summary: This unit teaches you to check whether an organisation is still heading in the right direction. You will learn how strategy is set out, how to track it with KPIs, dashboards and the balanced scorecard, how to scan the outside environment with PESTLE, SWOT and industry analysis, how to calculate and read results against targets, how to decide whether to persist, adjust or change course, and how to report to the board and bring people with you.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. Strategic direction is where an organisation says it is going and how it will get there. **Monitoring** is the regular tracking of progress. **Reviewing** is the deeper, less frequent question: *is this still the right direction?*

Markets, laws, technology and customers change. A strategy that was sound when it was approved can slowly stop fitting. Managers who track results and the outside world can correct the course in time. Managers who do not may find, years later, that the organisation has drifted away from its customers.
**Who it is for:** managers and senior supervisors in businesses, schools, health services and public bodies who report on strategic plans, run reviews or advise the board.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at work
rows: Explain strategic direction and why it is reviewed
Describe vision, mission, objectives and plans, and say how and when each is reviewed.
Use PESTLE, SWOT, industry analysis, benchmarking and stakeholder views to spot changes.
Choose a few KPIs, set targets, use a balanced scorecard and dashboard, and check the quality of the data.
Work out percentage of target, growth, market share and margins, and check every sum twice.
Find the causes of gaps, test the options and recommend persisting, adjusting or changing direction.
Keep a risk register with ratings, owners and reviews, and plan responses.
Write a clear board report, communicate changes and realign plans, budgets and people.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with business scenarios and calculations.
A **written paper**: short answers (exact terms and quick sums) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Group practicals**: a strategy review report from a case pack, and a board strategy review meeting role play. Each member has a named role.

blocks.note: Work every sum twice. Say which base you used, and whether you are giving a percentage or percentage points.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Strategy, monitoring and the review cycle

head: Level
What it says
Example
rows: What the organisation wants to become in the long term
To be the most trusted food distributor in the Caribbean
Its purpose today: what it does, for whom and how
We deliver safe, fresh food to Jamaican shops and hotels on time
What must be achieved, usually over three to five years
Win 400 new business customers; reach 15% market share
The choices about where to compete and how to win
Focus on hotels and supermarkets; invest in a cold chain
What each department will do this year, with budgets and targets
Warehouse: reduce picking errors to 1% by December

blocks.p: A strategy can be **deliberate** (planned and written) or **emergent** (it develops from many decisions and actions over time, and may differ from the plan). Reviews should look at both: what the plan says and what the organisation is really doing.

head: Point
Monitoring
Review
rows: Are we still going in the right direction?
Usually once a year, or when something big changes
Vision, mission, objectives, assumptions, markets, risks
Senior managers and the board, with input from staff and stakeholders
Corrective action to get back on track
Confirm, adjust or change the direction

blocks.p: A good timetable for a five-year plan: **track KPIs monthly, report to the board quarterly and review the plan yearly**. Review sooner if there is a major change, such as a new competitor, a new law, a big supplier problem or a sharp change in the economy.

ul: It **catches changes early**, when there is still time to adjust.
It stops **strategic drift**: a gradual move away from what customers and the market now need, as when an organisation keeps the same approach while customers move to online buying.
It tests the **assumptions** behind the plan, such as the exchange rate, interest rates, demand or supplier prices.
It keeps everyone's effort pointed at the **priorities**.
It builds **learning**: lessons are recorded and used in the next planning cycle.

blocks.note: When major changes occur in the market or in the organisation's purpose, also check whether the **mission statement** still fits.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Collect results and data on KPIs and milestones
Scan the outside environment and update the analysis
Compare results and assumptions with the plan to find the gaps
Find the causes and test the options
Recommend: persist, adjust or change direction
Report to the board and decide
Communicate, realign plans, budgets and people
Record lessons and start the next cycle

sections.title: Scanning the environment and the organisation

blocks.p: Environmental scanning is the **ongoing** work of collecting and studying information about outside trends that may affect the organisation. Use several tools, because each one shows a different part of the picture.

head: Factor
Questions to ask
Jamaican example
rows: Are there changes in government policy, taxes or public spending?
A new incentive for local manufacturers
What is happening to interest rates, inflation, the exchange rate and spending power?
A sharp rise in loan interest rates may reduce credit sales
Are customers' habits, ages or values changing?
More customers buying online and by mobile phone
What new technology could help or threaten us?
A new data protection law affecting an online seller
What are the climate and environmental risks and rules?
Hurricane damage to roads and warehouses; waste rules

blocks.p: SWOT sorts what you find. **Strengths** and **weaknesses** are **inside** the organisation. **Opportunities** and **threats** are **outside** it.

head: Source
Helpful
Harmful
rows: Strengths: a trusted brand, skilled staff, a good location
Weaknesses: old systems, high costs, key staff leaving
Opportunities: a new highway that cuts travel time to a main market, growing demand
Threats: a new competitor, rising costs, a change in law

blocks.note: A new highway is outside the firm and helps it, so it is an **opportunity**. A new rival is outside and harms it, so it is a **threat**. The firm's skilled staff are inside, so they are a **strength**.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Force
What it asks
If strong
rows: How hard do competitors fight for customers?
Prices and profits are pushed down
How easy is it for newcomers to start?
Can customers meet the need another way?
Can customers push prices down or switch easily?
Lower prices, more pressure on service
Can suppliers raise prices or refuse to supply?
Higher costs, risk of supply problems

head: Tool
What it does
rows: Compares where the business is now with where it aims to be, and shows what must change
Compares your results and methods with the best in the industry or region, for example staff turnover or guest scores
What the firm does better than rivals that customers value and rivals find hard to copy
Tests the strategy against several possible futures, such as visitor arrivals rising, staying flat or falling
Identifies the people and groups with an interest in the strategy (owners, staff, customers, suppliers, regulators, communities) and what they expect

blocks.p: Customers, staff and regulators see risks and needs that managers may miss. Gather their views through **surveys** (properly sampled and repeated over time), **interviews and focus groups**, **suggestion channels** and **meetings with team leaders**, who see problems on the ground early. Use more than one method and compare the results.

blocks.note: A firm whose profits are strong but whose neighbouring communities are complaining may be losing the trust it needs for its licence to operate and to grow. Strategic review looks at social and environmental performance as well as profit.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Measuring performance: KPIs, scorecards and calculations

blocks.p: A **key performance indicator (KPI)** is a measure chosen to track progress toward a key objective. Choose a **few** KPIs for each objective. A dashboard with 60 indicators hides what matters. A good KPI is clearly defined, linked to an objective, measurable with reliable data, owned by a named person, and has a target and a date.

head: Objective
A good KPI
rows: Be the most reliable delivery service in the Corporate Area
Percentage of parcels delivered on the promised day
Number of new business customers each quarter
Percentage of staff trained on the new system

head: Type
What it shows
Examples
rows: Results already achieved; you cannot change them now
Last year's profit, last quarter's sales, repeat bookings last year
Early signs of future results; you can still act
Guest satisfaction at check-out, enquiries and quotations, staff training completed

blocks.p: The **balanced scorecard** measures performance from four perspectives so that managers do not look only at money.

head: Perspective
Question
Example KPIs
rows: How do we look to owners?
What must we be excellent at?
Delivery on time, order errors, check-in time
Training hours per employee, staff turnover, new skills

blocks.p: Before you use figures from branches, check that they are **accurate, complete and comparable**. For example, if one branch counts complimentary rooms in occupancy and another does not, the two figures cannot be compared. Agree definitions and a template first.

head: Measure
Formula
Worked example
rows: Revenue J$800m, cost of sales J$520m: 280 ÷ 800 × 100 = 35%
Share falls from 18% to 15%: down 3 percentage points

blocks.note: **Percentage points** are not the same as **percent**. Share falling from 18% to 15% is a fall of 3 percentage points, but a fall of 16.7% in the share itself (3 ÷ 18). Always say which one you mean.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Always compare the percentage achieved with the **share of the time** that has passed. For example, 75% of a yearly target after nine months (9 ÷ 12 = 75% of the year) is exactly on pace; 60% would be behind.

A **dashboard** shows the KPIs on one page, with actual results beside the targets, usually coloured (green on track, amber warning, red off track), with a short comment on each red item. Use it to see at once where the organisation is ahead or behind.

sections.title: Analysing gaps and deciding what to do

blocks.h: From a gap to a cause

blocks.p: When a result is behind target, do not jump to a solution. **Find the cause first**. For example, if a security company has reached only 35% of its yearly sales target by mid-year and a rival is undercutting its prices, the manager should analyse the cause and the options, then propose a response.

flow: Describe the gap precisely (what, how big, since when)
Check that the data is right
Ask why, several times, and talk to the people closest to the work
Check whether the cause is inside the firm or outside it
Test each against data, costs, risks and capability

head: Choice
When it fits
Example
rows: The strategy is sound; the gap is temporary or caused by execution
A new service is behind plan only because of a late supplier
The objective is still right, but the method, timing or resources must change
Re-phase the opening of new stores because permits are slow
The market, law, technology or customers have changed so that the objective is no longer achievable or sensible
Close counters and move customers online as demand moves to digital channels

blocks.note: Test options against **data, costs, risks and capability**: can we do it, what will it cost, what could go wrong and do we have the people and skills?
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Every strategy rests on assumptions, such as a stable exchange rate, steady demand, supplier availability or the cost of shipping. In each review, list the assumptions and ask whether they still hold. If one has changed, costs and prices in the plan may be wrong.

blocks.h: Judging a decision after it is made

blocks.p: If a firm cut prices to win back market share, judge the result by comparing **market share, sales volume and margin** with the targets. A price cut that raises volume but destroys margin may not have worked.

A strategic risk is an event or condition that could stop the organisation reaching its objectives, such as relying on a single overseas supplier, losing a key customer or a change in law. Manage risks with a **strategic risk register**.

head: Column
What it holds
rows: What could go wrong, and why
Each rated, often 1 to 5; the **rating** is likelihood × impact (for example 4 × 3 = 12)
What is already done to reduce the risk
What more will be done, by when
When it will next be reviewed

ul: A **single supplier** risk can be reduced by developing other suppliers or a contingency plan.
Review the register at each quarterly meeting, and add new risks that the environmental scan reveals.
Rank by rating, so that the biggest risks get attention first.

blocks.p: If branch managers do not know how their targets link to the strategy, effort will not support the objectives. Make the link explicit: every unit target should be tied to a strategic objective.

head: Section
Content
rows: Key findings, the decisions needed and the recommendation, on the first page
KPI table or dashboard with targets, actual results and gaps
The main points from PESTLE, SWOT and stakeholder views
Why results differ from the plan
Options with evidence, expected benefits, costs and risks
The top items from the risk register
Actions, owners, dates and the next review date

blocks.p: **Evidence, expected benefits and risks** must support every recommendation. For a short board meeting (for example 15 minutes), lead with the key findings and the decisions needed, then support them with charts.
When the board changes an objective or direction, managers must:

ol: Explain what has changed, why it changed, and what it means for each group.
Update unit plans, budgets and targets so they match the new objectives.
Reallocate resources, for example move marketing money from a product being phased out to the new priorities.
Brief staff and stakeholders, with time for questions, and check understanding.
Provide training and support for any new roles or methods.
Monitor the changed plan with revised KPIs.

head: Audience
What they need to hear
rows: What changes for their job, when, and what support there will be
What changes in the service and how they will be looked after
What changes in orders and timing
The reasons, the risks and the expected results
Compliance and how the change affects them

blocks.note: Involve team leaders when reviewing how the strategy is working on the ground. They see problems early and make changes work.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A ministry, agency or municipal corporation also has a strategic or corporate plan, usually with a three-year cycle and performance targets set with the line ministry or the council. The review process is the same: track results, check changes in law and policy, and report to the board or council. Stakeholders include the public, councillors and other agencies.
After each annual review, **record the lessons learned** (what worked, what did not, and why) and use them in the next planning cycle.

ul: explain vision, mission, objectives, strategy and operational plans
tell monitoring from review, and set a sensible timetable for each
explain strategic drift and why regular review prevents it
use PESTLE, SWOT, Porter's five forces, gap analysis, benchmarking, core competence and scenario planning
gather and compare the views of stakeholders
choose a few good KPIs and tell leading from lagging indicators
place KPIs on the balanced scorecard's four perspectives
calculate percentage of target, growth, market share, margins and percentage points, and check each twice
find the cause of a gap and test options
decide whether to persist, adjust or change direction
keep a strategic risk register with ratings and owners
write a board report and communicate and realign after a change

terms: What the organisation wants to become in the long term
A major result to be achieved, usually over three to five years
Regular tracking of progress against targets
A deeper check of whether the direction is still right
A gradual move away from what the market needs, because the approach is not changed
A strategy that develops from actions and decisions over time
Ongoing study of outside trends that may affect the business
Political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors
A model of industry pressures: rivals, new entrants, substitutes, buyers, suppliers
A key performance indicator: a measure chosen to track progress
A measure of results already achieved
An early sign of future results
A framework that measures financial, customer, internal process, and learning and growth results
Comparing results and methods with the best performers
What a firm does better than rivals that is hard to copy
People and groups with an interest in the strategy
A planned step to bring results back on track

c1.title: A Kingston juice maker's year-two results
c1.text: A Kingston juice maker's five-year plan has a year-two sales target of J$2,000 million. Its sales were J$1,500 million last year and J$1,650 million this year, in a market worth J$8,250 million. Net profit was J$75 million last year and J$99 million this year. The gross margin target was 38% and the result was 36%.

c2.title: A north coast hotel group wants more repeat guests
c2.text: A hotel group on the north coast has a strategic objective to increase repeat guests. It tracks repeat bookings each year, guest satisfaction at check-out, average check-in time and the percentage of front-desk staff who complete service training. Two of its hotels record occupancy differently: one counts complimentary rooms and the other does not.

c3.title: A courier firm and a delivery app
c3.text: A courier firm in the Corporate Area has served small businesses for 25 years and has a loyal driver network and a trusted name. A new app-based delivery service has opened, offers lower prices and lets customers switch from one provider to another at no cost. The firm's sales to small businesses have fallen for three quarters, but management has not changed its approach.

c4.title: A municipal corporation's strategic plan
c4.text: A municipal corporation in Westmoreland has a three-year plan to improve market conditions for vendors. The risk register shows one risk, a delay in building the new market, rated 4 for likelihood and 3 for impact. The register does not say who is responsible for any risk. Vendors have not been consulted about the plan, and councillors want to know how to hear their views.

c5.title: A supermarket chain's expansion plan
c5.text: A supermarket chain in central Jamaica plans to open 10 new stores in five years. After two years it planned to have 4 open and has 3 open. Delays in getting approvals are the main reason. The strategy manager tracks the number of approved sites and permits as early signs, and the plan assumes costs for building materials will stay steady.

questions.q: What percentage of the year-two sales target did the juice maker reach?
questions.why: Percentage of target = actual ÷ target × 100 = 1,650 ÷ 2,000 × 100 = 82.5%. Check: 82.5% of 2,000 = 1,650.

questions.q: What was the growth in sales from last year to this year?
questions.why: Growth = (1,650 − 1,500) ÷ 1,500 × 100 = 150 ÷ 1,500 × 100 = 10%. The base is last year's figure, not this year's.

questions.q: What is the company's market share this year?
Net profit margin last year was 5% (75 ÷ 1,500). What happened to it this year?
o: It rose by 1 percent, to 6 percent
It rose by 1 percentage point, to 6%
It rose by 24 percentage points, to 99%
It fell by 1 percentage point, to 4%
questions.why: This year: 99 ÷ 1,650 × 100 = 6%. The difference between 5% and 6% is 1 percentage point. (It is a 20% rise in the margin itself, so always say which you mean.)

questions.q: The gross margin was 36% against a 38% target. How far behind target is it?
o: 2 percentage points
5.3 percentage points
38 percentage points
questions.why: The gap is 38% − 36% = 2 percentage points. A gap between two percentages is expressed in percentage points.

questions.q: Which of the hotel group's measures is a lagging indicator?
o: Guest satisfaction scores at check-out
The share of front-desk staff trained in service
The number of guest complaints resolved in 24 hours
The number of repeat bookings in the last year
questions.why: A lagging indicator records results already achieved. Last year's repeat bookings cannot now be changed, while the other measures give early signs that managers can still act on.

questions.q: On the balanced scorecard, under which perspective does 'average check-in time' fit best?
o: Financial
Customer
Internal process
Learning and growth
questions.why: How quickly the hotel carries out a core process (check-in) is an internal process measure. Guest satisfaction would be a customer measure, and training would be learning and growth.

questions.q: Why is it a problem that the two hotels record occupancy differently?
o: Occupancy is not a useful measure for any hotel
The hotel with the higher figure is performing better
Figures cannot be compared until the definitions match
The board should use only one hotel's figure
questions.why: Data used in a review must be accurate, complete and comparable. Agree one definition, then restate the figures so they can be compared.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the group using only a few indicators for its repeat-guest objective?
o: So that the group can avoid setting any targets
So managers can see clearly whether it is on track
So that every department has the same indicators
So that the results cannot be audited later
questions.why: A few well-chosen KPIs linked to the objective keep attention on what matters. Too many indicators hide the important signals.

questions.q: In a SWOT analysis, where does the courier firm's trusted name and driver network belong?
o: Strength
Opportunity
Weakness
Threat
questions.why: Strengths are inside the organisation and help it. A trusted brand and a loyal driver network are internal advantages.

questions.q: Customers can switch to the app at no cost. Which of Porter's five forces does this strengthen?
o: The bargaining power of suppliers
The rivalry among only the existing couriers
The cost of raw materials
The bargaining power of buyers
questions.why: When it is easy to switch and prices are lower elsewhere, customers can push prices down or leave. That is strong buyer power.

questions.q: Sales have fallen for three quarters, but management has not changed its approach. What does this suggest?
o: The firm is following a successful emergent strategy
The fall is a one-off event that needs no action
The strategy needs no review until the end of the plan
The firm may be showing strategic drift
questions.why: Strategic drift is a gradual loss of fit between the firm and its market when the approach is not reviewed. Three quarters of decline is a clear signal for early review.

questions.q: Which step should come first in the strategy review of this situation?
o: Cut prices below the app's prices straight away
Close the small-business service and focus elsewhere
Find out why small customers are leaving, using data and their views
Advertise more without first checking the cause
questions.why: Analyse the cause before choosing a response. Price, convenience, service and technology are different problems with different answers.

questions.q: The risk of a delay to the new market is rated 4 for likelihood and 3 for impact. What is its rating?
questions.why: Rating = likelihood × impact = 4 × 3 = 12. Adding the two scores (7) is not the usual method.

questions.q: What is the most important thing the register is missing?
o: A named owner for each risk, with actions and dates
More risks that are unlikely to happen at all
A longer description of the plan's history
A list of all the councillors and their wards
questions.why: A risk without an owner is not managed. Each entry needs a person responsible, an action and a date for review.

questions.q: Which method would best gather vendors' views for the strategic review?
o: A properly sampled survey or focus groups over time
One councillor's opinion of what vendors want
Only the complaints that happen to reach the office
Waiting until the market has been built to ask them
questions.why: Stakeholder views are most reliable when gathered systematically from a representative group and repeated. Single opinions and chance complaints can be biased.

questions.q: What percentage of the year-two milestone (4 stores) has the chain achieved?
questions.why: 3 ÷ 4 × 100 = 75%. Check: 75% of 4 = 3. Compare with the five-year target: 3 of 10 is 30%, after 40% of the time has passed.

questions.q: Delays in approvals are the main cause of the shortfall. Which response is best?
o: Cancel the expansion objective and review again
Ignore the delay and keep the old dates
Adjust the timeline and apply for approvals earlier
Open stores before approvals to catch up
questions.why: The objective is still sound and the cause is a process delay, so the plan should be adjusted: re-phase the openings and apply for approvals sooner. Opening without approvals is unlawful.

questions.q: The plan assumes building material costs will stay steady. What should the strategy review do?
o: Leave the assumption because the board approved it
Check whether the assumption holds and update costs
Remove the assumption from the plan altogether
Assume that the costs will fall instead of rise
questions.why: A review must test the assumptions behind the plan. If costs have risen, the budget and the pace of expansion may need to change.

questions.q: A strategy review report runs to 40 pages and its recommendation is on page 38. The board says it is hard to use. What is the best improvement?
o: Move the KPI tables to the very end of the report
Open with a short summary of findings and the decisions needed
Remove the risks so that the report is shorter
Add more background on the firm's history first
questions.why: Board members need the key findings and the decisions required first, with the detail behind them. A summary on the first page makes the report usable.
